content: A brownout, also referred to as a grey-out, is a temporary loss of vision characterized by a perceived dimming of light, often accompanied by a brownish tint and a reduction in peripheral vision. This phenomenon is typically a precursor to fainting or a blackout and is caused by hypoxia, a drop in blood pressure, or restricted blood flow to the brain. It is commonly experienced when standing up suddenly, particularly in individuals who are ill, hungover, or suffering from low blood pressure or shock. Recovery from a brownout is usually rapid and can often be reversed by lying down. A brownout can be intentionally induced, though inadvisably, through hyperventilation, as described in the context of the choking game, which involves self-induced hypocapnia. Hyperventilation may also unintentionally lead to a brownout, as seen in cases of shallow water blackout. Additionally, brownouts are experienced by aircraft pilots subjected to high positive G-forces, such as during a pull-up into a loop or a tight turn. These forces cause blood to pool in the lower extremities, reducing blood pressure in the brain. This is the opposite of a redout, which involves a reddening of vision caused by negative G-forces, such as during an outside loop when the aircraft's nose is pushed downward. Redouts are potentially dangerous and can result in retinal damage or hemorrhagic stroke. High-performance aircraft pilots can increase their resistance to brownouts by wearing a G-suit, which helps prevent blood from pooling in the lower limbs. However, no suit currently exists to counteract redouts. In both cases, symptoms can be immediately alleviated by reducing pressure on the aircraft's joystick. Prolonged or intense G-forces, however, can quickly lead to G-LOC (G-force-induced Loss of Consciousness). Brownouts are also commonly experienced by roller coaster riders. Many roller coasters subject riders to high positive G-forces, particularly in vertical loops and helices. However, roller coasters rarely generate sufficient negative G-forces to induce redouts, as low-G elements are typically designed to simulate weightlessness. Grey-outs may also occur after donating blood, as the loss of blood volume can lead to a drop in blood pressure and insufficient blood flow to the brain. However, the onset of such grey-outs is usually gradual and can be prevented by lying down, which allows blood to flow to the brain without working against gravity.
